title: Interactive Digital Marketing Dashboard
text:
Project Overview
This individual project transformed a digital marketing campaign dataset into two reporting tools: a static Quarto dashboard and an interactive Shiny application.
The dataset contained 8,000 customer records covering demographics, campaign types, website engagement, email activity, purchase history, loyalty points, and conversion.

title: Interactive Digital Marketing Dashboard
text:
Dashboard Features
The Quarto dashboard presented:

Total customers and overall conversion rate
Customer age and income distributions
Campaign-type performance
Website visits and time on site
Email engagement
Previous purchases and loyalty points

The Shiny application allowed users to filter the data by date, campaign type, and gender. Users could also select variables for an interactive Plotly chart and review filtered records in a searchable table.

title: Interactive Digital Marketing Dashboard
text:
What I Learned
This project helped me understand the difference between a fixed report and an interactive analytical application. The static dashboard communicates the main results quickly, while the Shiny application allows users to explore specific customer groups and marketing scenarios.

title: Customer Conversion Prediction
text:
Project Overview
This individual project applied supervised machine learning to predict whether a customer would convert after exposure to a digital marketing campaign.
The analysis followed a complete modeling workflow that included data preparation, training and testing splits, preprocessing, cross-validation, model comparison, and feature-importance analysis.

title: Customer Conversion Prediction
text:
Models Compared
Two classification models were evaluated:

Logistic regression
Random forest with 500 decision trees

Because the outcome was imbalanced, ROC AUC was used as the primary model-selection metric instead of relying only on accuracy.

title: Customer Conversion Prediction
text:
Key Findings
The random forest achieved the stronger overall discrimination:

Random forest ROC AUC: 0.825
Logistic regression ROC AUC: 0.801
Logistic regression accuracy: 89.4%
Random forest accuracy: 89.2%

The random forest was selected because ROC AUC provided a more reliable performance measure for the imbalanced conversion outcome.
Pages per visit, time on site, advertising spend, and click-through rate were among the most influential predictors. Other engagement measures, including email activity, previous purchases, and loyalty points, also contributed to prediction.

title: Customer Conversion Prediction
text:
Business Value
The results demonstrate how predictive models can help marketers identify high-potential customers and prioritize meaningful engagement signals. The project also reinforced that feature importance indicates predictive usefulness, not causation.

title: Amazon Weekly Revenue Forecasting
text:
Project Overview
This group project examined how historical Amazon transaction data could be used to forecast weekly revenue. The original order-level data was aggregated into weekly totals, creating a time series that could support an 8- to 12-week business forecast.
My primary contributions included developing the forecasting methodology, writing the R code, comparing candidate models, and interpreting the forecast results.

title: Amazon Weekly Revenue Forecasting
text:
Analytical Approach
We compared two forecasting methods:

Exponential smoothing, or ETS
Time-series regression with pricing and customer-feedback predictors

The final 12 weeks of data were reserved as a test set. Model performance was evaluated using RMSE and MAPE so that the forecasts could be compared on unseen data.

title: Amazon Weekly Revenue Forecasting
text:
Key Findings
The time-series regression model performed better than the ETS model:

Regression MAPE: 3.34%
ETS MAPE: 6.60%
Regression RMSE: 12,100
ETS RMSE: 22,906

Weekly revenue was relatively stable, although short-term fluctuations were present. Review count was the most useful predictor in the regression model, while discount percentage and customer rating were not statistically significant.

title: Amazon Weekly Revenue Forecasting
text:
Business Value
The selected model could support short-term inventory planning, revenue targets, budget allocation, and cash-flow decisions. The findings also showed that businesses should validate discount strategies instead of assuming that greater discounting will automatically increase revenue.

title: Customer Demographics and Conversion
text:
Project Overview
This analysis was my assigned analytics objective within a digital marketing campaign group project. I examined whether age, gender, and income were associated with customer conversion and whether these variables could support customer targeting.
The dataset included 8,000 customer records and a binary conversion outcome.

title: Customer Demographics and Conversion
text:
Analytical Approach
I used exploratory visualizations, logistic regression, and a random forest model. Because approximately 88% of customers converted, accuracy alone could provide a misleading picture of model performance.
The analysis therefore emphasized ROC AUC, balanced accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity.

title: Customer Demographics and Conversion
text:
Key Findings
Age, gender, and income showed substantial overlap between converters and non-converters. The better-performing demographic model produced:

ROC AUC: 0.539
Balanced accuracy: 0.501

These results were close to chance-level performance, showing that demographic variables alone were not sufficient for identifying customers who were likely to convert.

title: Customer Demographics and Conversion
text:
Business Value
The findings suggest that marketers should prioritize behavioral and engagement data when developing targeting strategies. Demographic information may still be useful for audience description, segmentation, and fairness checks, but it should not be treated as the primary source of conversion predictions.
